newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S.-EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-EU trumpet breakthrough on trade.

text.p: The United States and the European Union said on Wednesday they had cleared the way for a deal allowing their businesses once-for-all safety standards approval in five product categories worth $40 billion a year.

"We feel that we have a breakthrough and we hope that it will lead to an agreement in the next few days," U.S. President Bill Clinton said after EU-U.S. talks with Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok and European Commission President Jacques Santer.
A U.S. official said ahead of set-piece talks on Wednesday that the Mutual Recognition Agreements (MRAs) on product standards had been sorted within the last hours.
The official said MRAs would reduce marketing costs for telecommunications equipment, information-technology products, pharmaceuticals, medical devices and pleasure boats.
Kok said talks had also cracked bilateral differences on veterinary inspections for poultry meat.
"We also reached an agreement on veterinary inspection, thus resolving a trade conflict that might might otherwise have arisen on the export of meat products," he said.

Kok said agreements were also struck on controlling trade in narcotics precursor ingredients -- key materials used in the manufacture of drugs like ecstasy -- and on customs cooperation between U.S. and EU police forces fighting drugs and terrorism.
While the customs cooperation and drugs precursors deals were flagged well in advance of Wednesday's summit, the one on MRAs came as more of a surprise.
Although both Kok and Santer echoed Clinton's assessment of an MRA deal being but a few days away, a European Commission spokesman warned that any text still had to go to EU capitals.
MRAS are expected to cut manufacturers' marketing costs by as much as 10 percent by allowing each party to recognise the other's testing, inspection and certification procedures.
The U.S. official said the final sticking points concerned U.S. Food and Drug Administration regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

He said the FDA was legally prohibited from ceding final inspection authority over the manufacturing of these devices, but as a practical matter would "not feel the need to do so" in the case of already-approved products manufactured under E.U. standards.
